headline: Zejian Wang and co-authors measured a default NCCL reduce-scatter slowing a concurrent matrix multiply by 69 per cent, because the collective and the multiply contend for the same GPU multiprocessors — overlapping communication with computation does not make it free.

items.title: Evaporating niobium with a 533-watt laser instead of a crucible
items.dek: Yifei Yan and co-authors deposited superconducting niobium films by focusing a 533-watt continuous-wave fibre laser onto a bare niobium pellet — no crucible, no plasma, no substrate heating — and measured a superconducting transition temperature only 10 millikelvin below bulk niobium.
items.why_it_matters: Refractory metals evaporate only at temperatures no crucible survives, which is why niobium is normally sputtered or electron-beam evaporated. Heating a 500-micrometre spot of the metal itself makes the source its own container, removing both usual contamination routes — crucible material and plasma-accelerated ions — at the same time. The payoff is measurable rather than argued: a residual-resistivity ratio of 5.71, roughly 1.5 to 2.5 times what comparable unheated films reach. The cost is a growth rate of 0.19 ångström per second.
items.background_md: Thin metal films are laid down either by knocking atoms off a target with a plasma, which is sputtering, or by boiling the metal and letting the vapour condense, which is evaporation. Each carries a signature contamination. A plasma accelerates ions into the growing film and changes its microstructure and residual stress; an evaporation source has to sit in a crucible whose own material dissolves into the melt. Electrical purity is how the result gets graded, and for a superconductor that means two numbers: how close the transition temperature sits to the bulk value, and the residual-resistivity ratio.
items.deeper_md:
The run lasted 20 minutes at 0.19 Å/s from a free-standing 99.95% Nb pellet press-fit in a molybdenum holder, 8 cm from an unheated, unrotated c-plane sapphire substrate, at a 2×10⁻⁸ Torr base pressure. The film came out 22.47 ± 0.05 nm thick — 19.77 nm of Nb under 2.70 nm of Nb₂O₅ — with 0.23 ± 0.02 nm RMS roughness, 21.60 ± 0.05 µΩ·cm at room temperature, RRR 5.71, a transition at 9.24 K against a 9.25 K bulk value, and a 29 mK transition width.

Three caveats, all stated by the authors. Only two films were grown; the second landed at 9.05 K, RRR 5.44 and a 41 mK width, and fell to 8.78 K after two months in storage, probably from surface oxidation. The 0.19 Å/s rate is below the 0.34 Å/s reported at 250 W in earlier thermal-laser-evaporation work, which they attribute to radiative and conductive losses through the larger target and its press-fit mount. And an unexplained Nb(222) reflection carries about −2.19% out-of-plane compression.

Nobody disputes the measurement yet because there is nothing to dispute: the comparison against sputtered and e-beam films is drawn from the literature, not from films grown side by side in one chamber.

glossary.definition: A metal's room-temperature resistivity divided by its resistivity just above the superconducting transition; it rises with purity and crystal quality, because impurity and defect scattering is what survives at low temperature.
The temperature at which a superconductor's resistance falls to zero; thin films sit below the bulk value because surfaces, disorder and oxide layers suppress it.
One whose evaporation temperature is high enough that a crucible holding it would evaporate too, which is why such metals are normally sputtered or electron-beam evaporated.
Deposition rate in tenths of a nanometre per second; 0.19 Å/s is about 1.1 nm a minute, so a 20 nm film takes a third of an hour.

items.fab_angle: The operational lesson is one any tool with a window in the beam path shares: niobium landing on the chamber mirror forced the laser power up run after run until the coating plateaued. A maskless stepper's final optic faces the same drift, which is the argument for putting in-situ power monitoring after the window rather than before it.

sources.title: Thermal laser evaporation of superconducting Nb films
Thermal laser evaporation of elements from across the periodic table

items.title: A thermoreflectance model that stops pretending the spot is infinite
items.dek: Abhishek Pathak and co-authors at Carnegie Mellon derived a heat-diffusion model for frequency-domain thermoreflectance — reading thermal properties from how a heated surface's reflectivity lags a modulated laser — that accounts for a finite beam radius, and showed the usual infinite-radius approximation only converges above roughly 100 micrometres.
items.why_it_matters: The standard analysis treats the heating beam as infinitely wide, which makes the measured phase lag independent of spot size; the new model shows predicted phase rising with spot radius, against the 2.3 to 5.0 micrometres these measurements actually used. Fitting with the right geometry then surfaces a physical result instead of absorbing it into the fit: the in-plane thermal conductivity of the gold lines themselves falls by roughly half as linewidth drops from 1,024 to 172 nanometres.
items.background_md: Thermoreflectance measures heat without touching anything. A modulated laser warms a metal film, a second laser reads that film's reflectivity, which shifts slightly with temperature, and the phase lag between heating and reading is fitted to a heat-diffusion model to extract thermal conductivity and the conductance across buried interfaces. Nothing is imaged; everything is inferred, so the method's accuracy is the model's accuracy, and every geometric simplification becomes a systematic error in the number reported. Patterned surfaces are where the simplifications bite hardest, because heat then spreads differently along the pattern than across it.
items.deeper_md:
The targets were about 75 nm of gold over 5 nm of chromium: lines 172, 524 and 1,024 nm wide on amorphous SiO₂ and 234, 548 and 1,052 nm wide on c-plane sapphire, with gaps near 150–180 nm. Pump and probe spots measured 2.3–5.0 µm at 1/e², modulated from 100 kHz to 5 MHz.

Fitted thermal boundary conductance landed at 37–39 MW/m²·K for Au-Cr on SiO₂ and 286–392 MW/m²·K on sapphire, against a literature 390 ± 70; sapphire's fitted conductivity matched its bulk 38 ± 2 W/m·K. Transport stayed diffusive throughout, because the phonon mean free path in amorphous SiO₂ is about 1 nm and roughly 90% of sapphire's conductivity comes from paths under 100 nm — which is precisely why the work can serve as the baseline for later experiments hunting for suppression.

Two limits the authors name. Modelling the gaps as gold with zero in-plane conductivity shifts the phase by under 1.1°, worth 0.3% in sapphire conductivity and 2.9% in boundary conductance. And overexposure during patterning left the lines about 20 nm too wide on SiO₂ and 35–50 nm too wide on sapphire, so the nominal linewidths are not the printed ones.

glossary.definition: A measurement in which a modulated laser heats a surface and a second laser reads the temperature swing through a small change in reflectivity, with the phase lag between the two carrying the thermal information.
Heat flow per unit area per degree across the interface between two materials, in MW/m²·K; it is finite because the lattice vibrations on either side have mismatched spectra.
The average distance a lattice vibration travels before scattering; once it exceeds the heated spot or the feature size, heat stops obeying the diffusion equation.
The radius at which a Gaussian beam's intensity has dropped to about 13.5% of its peak — the conventional way to quote a laser spot size.

items.fab_angle: The nuisance they document is reproducible in a teaching lab: pump light leaking through the grating gaps and reflecting off the back of the substrate corrupted the phase until glycerin was applied to the wafer's rear face. Any optical measurement on a transparent substrate, resist thickness by reflectometry included, has the same back-surface problem and the same fix.

sources.title: Analytical framework for interpreting thermoreflectance measurements of nanoline gratings under finite spot illumination
Thermoreflectance-Based Techniques for Micro- and Nanoscale Thermophysical Property Measurements

items.title: Friction on diamond tracks one number: bonds per square nanometre
items.dek: Enrico Pedretti and Maria Clelia Righi fitted a machine-learning interatomic potential for carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and silicon, slid diamond against amorphous silicon nitride for 70 nanometres of simulated travel, and found shear stress rising linearly with the count of covalent bonds formed across the sliding interface.
items.why_it_matters: Surface chemistry stops being a qualitative story once there is a slope, and the slope is about 0.7 gigapascals per bond per square nanometre. Hydrogen-and-hydroxyl termination keeps the interface bond-free up to roughly 1 gigapascal of contact pressure, with shear stress near zero; strip it and 18 to 24 bonds per square nanometre form at once, shear saturates at 7 to 8 gigapascals, and the sliding plane leaves the interface entirely to move inside the softer nitride. Two wear regimes with a measurable boundary, not one continuum.
items.background_md: Friction between two hard solids, at the scale where a polishing slurry does its work, is less about roughness than about whether atoms on the two surfaces bond to each other. A clean covalent surface carries dangling bonds that will react with whatever they touch, including the counter-surface, and every bond that forms has to be broken again before sliding can continue. Capping those bonds with hydrogen or hydroxyl groups is what keeps diamond tools and diamond coatings slippery, and it is why one material's friction changes between humid air and vacuum.
items.deeper_md:
The potential used a MACE architecture trained on 253 systems, 30,423 configurations and about 14.8 million atomic environments, reaching 2.7 meV/atom energy and 88.8 meV/Å force mean absolute error in the production model, with H₂, H₂O and O₂ dissociation barriers on diamond within a few tenths of an electronvolt of the reference density-functional values.

Sliding ran at 10 m/s for 7 ns — 70 nm total — over about 7,000 atoms, at normal loads of 0.1, 1, 10 and 23 GPa, the last chosen to equal silicon nitride's hardness. In the bond-controlled regime a linear fit of shear stress against interfacial bond density gives R² = 0.92 and a slope near 0.7 GPa per nm⁻². Shear localisation widens with load: under 1 Å of slip zone at 0.1–1 GPa, 1.4 Å at 10 GPa, and about 11 Å at 23 GPa, where the amorphous nitride flows in Couette fashion.

The objections are the standard ones for the method, and the authors raise them first. Tensile tests ran at 10⁹ s⁻¹ strain rate, orders above experiment, so plasticity is qualitative. The 70 nm travel bounds the passivation claim. And chemical mechanical planarization appears only as a stated future target: the diamond-silica interface that would matter there was trained for, not run.

glossary.definition: A fitted function returning the energy and forces of an atomic configuration, standing in for a quantum-mechanical calculation so that millions of atoms over nanoseconds become affordable.
Capping a surface's unsatisfied covalent bonds with hydrogen or hydroxyl groups so it stops reacting with whatever it is pressed against.
The force per unit area resisting sliding, here in gigapascals; divided by the normal pressure it would give the friction coefficient this paper deliberately does not report.
The unit for force error in a fitted potential — millielectronvolts per ångström; 88.8 meV/Å is the typical error on each force component in the model used for production runs.

sources.title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica
MACE: Higher Order Equivariant Message Passing Neural Networks for Fast and Accurate Force Fields

items.title: A pin is a shape, not a point, and analog placers rounded it off
items.dek: Bingyang Liu, Xiaohan Gao, Souradip Poddar and David Pan built an analog placement tool that picks where on each device's terminal metal a wire will actually land while it is still deciding where to put the devices; pinning that choice to the device centre instead costs up to 13 decibels of common-mode rejection on their amplifier benchmarks.
items.why_it_matters: Analytical placers score a candidate layout with half-perimeter wirelength computed from device centres, which quietly assumes every net connects at the middle of each device — a point no router will ever use. The consequence is not cosmetic. On their clocked comparator, placing with the connection point pinned to the centre gave 135.1 picoseconds of delay against 109.9 with it free, and routed wirelength across the three amplifiers fell 3.3 to 8.4 per cent once the two decisions were made together.
items.background_md: Automatic placement decides where each device sits on a die by minimising a differentiable stand-in for how much wire the router will later need. That stand-in matters more than it sounds. An analog circuit's performance is set by the parasitic resistance and capacitance of those wires and by how closely matched pairs of devices track each other, so a placement that scores well on the proxy and routes badly reappears after extraction as lost gain, lost rejection or added delay. Digital placement tolerates the approximation because its figure of merit is timing slack over millions of cells; analog does not, because a handful of nets carry everything.
items.deeper_md:
The move is making the connection point differentiable. Each pin gets an angle φ mapped onto a superellipse fitted to its terminal's bounding box, so the access point slides continuously around the terminal and gradients reach both device coordinates and angles. The objective blends centre-based and access-point wirelength as W_mix = (1 − α)·W_base + α·W_ap, with α pinned at zero until a smoothed overlap signal says the devices have separated enough for the angles to mean anything.

Four benchmarks in TSMC N40 — three operational transconductance amplifiers of 26 to 50 devices, plus an 18-device comparator, 69 to 177 access-point variables — extracted in Calibre and simulated in Spectre. Against the MAGICAL flow, OTA2 gains 7.4 dB of gain and 15.9 dB of CMRR; the ablation assigns about 4 dB of gain and 1.4 to 13.0 dB of CMRR to the access points specifically. Placement completes in 7 to 62 seconds single-threaded.

What "comparable layout area" covers over: APPlace is larger than MAGICAL on all three amplifiers — 3,113 against 2,759 µm² on OTA1 — and MAGICAL wins on OTA3 phase margin and comparator energy per cycle. Four circuits, one deterministic run each, symmetry the only constraint modelled.

glossary.definition: The specific spot on a device terminal's metal where the router lands a wire; terminals are extended shapes, so the choice changes the routed path and the parasitics it carries.
Half the perimeter of the bounding box enclosing a net's pins — the standard differentiable stand-in for how much wire a router will eventually use.
How much more strongly an amplifier responds to the difference between its inputs than to both moving together, in decibels; layout-induced mismatch is what degrades it.
The stage after continuous optimisation that pushes overlapping devices onto legal positions without destroying the arrangement the optimiser found.

items.fab_angle: The repository is GPL-3.0 Rust with no solver and no C++ dependency, and it ships four abstract benchmarks that run with no PDK at all — ota2 is 49 devices, 35 nets and 24 symmetry pairs. A club designing its own cells can rerun the access-point ablation without TSMC N40 access, which is the rare case where an EDA paper is checkable on a laptop.

items.title: Testing a low-precision GPU kernel without guessing a tolerance
items.dek: Xinyi Shi's numoracle derives a per-element acceptance window for a GPU kernel's output from the reference program's declared rounding plan rather than from hand-picked absolute and relative tolerances, and reports no false alarms across 33,960 runs of correct kernels on each of two GPUs.
items.why_it_matters: A tolerance is one number standing in for an error budget that actually depends on the input, the number format and the order of accumulation, so it is wrong in both directions at once — loose enough to let real faults through, tight enough to reject correct code when the input distribution moves. Among 400 tuned configurations, those held to at most 1 per cent false alarms caught at most 31 of 53 injected faults where the derived bound caught 50.
items.background_md: Floating-point addition is not associative, so two correct implementations of the same reduction return different answers, and a fast GPU kernel is almost never bit-identical to the obvious reference. Testing therefore compares with a tolerance: accept if the difference falls within some absolute and relative bound. Choosing that bound is left to the engineer, and the correct value depends on how many roundings happened, in which formats, and in what order — none of which the test is told. As precision drops, the gap between a legitimate difference and a bug narrows until the tolerance, not the code, decides the verdict.
items.deeper_md:
Each value travels as a shadow element: the exact reference value, a deterministic residual bound, and random error components each tagged with an axis key and a sub-Gaussian proxy. The axis key is the mechanism. Multiply 4,096 ones by a single bf16 scalar and sum them: treat the 4,096 errors as independent and the bound comes out at 1.42, below the true error of 8, so every correct run is flagged; key the scalar's error to the broadcast axis so those errors add coherently and the bound is 17.1.

A second check covers truncating stores. A symmetric bound on the output-minus-reference difference can admit a neighbouring representable value near a rounding boundary, so numoracle also demands the output lie inside the rounding interval of the reference plus or minus its bound. In the main campaign across 13 Triton operators that check killed no extra fault, which the paper says plainly.

Soundness rests on four assumptions and the first is the one to argue with: rounding errors are modelled as mean-zero conditional on earlier errors. On deterministic hardware with a fixed input they are fixed numbers, not random — the answer offered is a separate fixed-input mode that drops the assumption for a worst-case enclosure.

glossary.definition: The absolute and relative tolerances a numerical test compares against; a result passes when the difference is within atol plus rtol times the magnitude of the reference value.
Half the spacing between representable numbers at a given magnitude in a given format — the largest error one correctly-rounded operation can introduce.
A declaration of which format each intermediate value is rounded to and which format each reduction accumulates in; numoracle takes this as the specification in place of a tolerance.
A deliberately broken copy of the code under test; the share of mutants a test suite rejects measures how much of the fault space it can actually see.

sources.title: Beyond atol and rtol: Sound Test Oracles for Low-Precision GPU Kernels

items.title: The copy between tensor and collective buffer was 6.4% of the step
items.dek: Zejian Wang and co-authors measured what it costs for PyTorch FSDP2 to keep parameters as separate per-parameter tensors while its collective communication wants one flat rank-major buffer: converting between the two layouts is 6.4 per cent of step time training Llama-3.1 70B at 8,192 tokens per GPU.
items.why_it_matters: The copy is not the interesting part; what the copy competes for is. A default NCCL reduce-scatter runs as a kernel on the GPU's streaming multiprocessors, and the same measurement shows it slowing a concurrent matrix multiply that would otherwise finish in a single wave by 69 per cent, so communication costs compute time even when it is perfectly overlapped. Folding layout into the collective's addressing and pushing transport onto copy engines and NVSwitch multicast cuts reduce-scatter multiprocessor time by 12.5 to 14.5 times.
items.background_md: Training a model too large for one accelerator means every device holds a slice of the parameters and fetches the rest when it needs them. Fully-sharded data parallelism does this by splitting the usual all-reduce in two: an all-gather before a layer computes, and a reduce-scatter of that layer's gradients afterwards. Those collectives are not free rides on the network. On an NVIDIA GPU they are kernels occupying streaming multiprocessors — the same units the matrix multiplies need — so the standard assumption that overlapping communication with computation hides it holds only when the two do not contend for the same hardware.
items.deeper_md:
FSDP2 exposes each sharded parameter as a DTensor sharded on dimension 0, so gradients arrive as separate per-parameter tensors in bfloat16, while NCCL's collectives want one contiguous rank-major buffer — in float32 if the reduction is to be done in float32, which the PyTorch documentation recommends because gradients vary widely between ranks. Something has to pack and unpack, and that something is a copy kernel.

TIDE instead hands the collective its final addresses. The all-gather writes shards straight into parameter storage over NVSwitch multicast with paced recursive-doubling RDMA between nodes, using no multiprocessors for transport or placement; the reduce-scatter accumulates bfloat16 gradients directly into float32 shards, a mixed-precision mode NCCL does not offer, using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks node-locally.

The best case, on 64 GPUs, is Qwen3-30B-A3B at 16K tokens per GPU: step time falls 27.1% against stock FSDP2, but only 6.0% against FSDP2 with symmetric memory — and the second number is the honest one, because most of the easy win is already available. Peak memory sits 4.7 GiB below that baseline. All of it was measured on stock NCCL 2.31.2 over at most eight nodes with eight GPUs per NVSwitch domain and one RDMA rail each; parameter groups outside the stated contracts fall back to ordinary collectives, CUDA-graph capture is not supported yet, and the multicast path has no equivalent on a fabric without multimem.

glossary.definition: The two collectives sharded training is built from: one assembles every rank's slice into a full tensor on every rank, the other sums a tensor across ranks and leaves each rank one slice of the sum.
The GPU's compute block; both matrix-multiply kernels and NCCL's communication kernels execute on them, which is why the two contend.
A DMA unit on the GPU that moves memory independently of the streaming multiprocessors, so a transfer it performs does not consume compute throughput.
A buffer ordered so all of rank 0's data precedes all of rank 1's — convenient for a collective, and not the byte order a per-parameter tensor wants.

sources.title: The Endgame of FSDP Communication: Layout-Aware Collectives on Copy Engines, RDMA, and NVSwitch
Getting Started with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2)

items.title: Most of multi-token prediction's gradient is noise, and can be deleted
items.dek: Jayden Teoh split the gradient that multi-token prediction — training a language model to predict several future tokens at once — sends back into its shared trunk, and found roughly 80 per cent of it is a residual term whose signal-to-noise ratio is about four times worse than the useful part.
items.why_it_matters: Writing the decomposition out exactly turns a tuning question into a deletion. The useful half is the gradient of a KL divergence pulling each extra head toward the model's own next-token distribution; the residual is next-token cross-entropy against a single sampled target, and its one-hot sampling noise never shrinks with scale. Routing only the KL half through the trunk is one line of PyTorch, adds no parameters and no measurable throughput cost, and the signal-to-noise gap it removes widens from 4.1× to 4.6× between 167 million and 1.2 billion parameters.
items.background_md: A language model is normally trained to predict one token at a time. Multi-token prediction bolts small extra heads onto the shared trunk, each predicting a token further ahead, as an auxiliary task — and those heads get reused at inference as the draft model for speculative decoding, guessing several tokens cheaply so the full model can verify them in one pass. Because the auxiliary loss shares a trunk with the main objective, whatever gradient it sends back either helps the main task or fights it, and nothing in the standard formulation says which.
items.deeper_md:
For head k the hard cross-entropy gradient factors exactly into Wᵀ(p − q) + Wᵀ(q − x), where q is the position-aligned next-token distribution, p is the head's own distribution, x is the one-hot sampled target and W the shared output head. The first term is the gradient of KL(stop-grad(q) ‖ p). The second is simply the next-token cross-entropy gradient against the data, and it splits again into a next-token error that shrinks with scale and sampling noise that does not.

Recovering the first term without materialising vocabulary-sized logit matrices is the trick: add stop-grad(h) − h to the next-token hidden states, numerically zero in the forward pass, which injects the negation of the residual backward. In code that is `h0[:, k:] += hk.detach() - hk`.

The mechanism is clearer than the payoff, and that is worth saying. Over 31.5 billion tokens of FineWeb-Edu, speculative-decoding speedup at 1.2B parameters moves 1.74 → 1.76 and average zero-shot accuracy 56.80 → 57.31; LAMBADA perplexity gets worse at 167M and 332M before turning. Everything stops at 1.2B on one dataset, so the claim that the interference grows at frontier scale is extrapolation from four points.

glossary.definition: A measure of how far one probability distribution sits from another; minimising it against a frozen copy of a model's own output is what self-distillation means.
Generating several tokens with a cheap draft model and checking them in one forward pass of the full model, so the accepted tokens arrive almost free.
Marking a tensor so it still contributes its value in the forward pass but passes no gradient backward — the standard way to freeze a target.
Here, the ratio of a gradient component's mean to its variability across batches; a component with low SNR moves the weights mostly at random.

sources.title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction

foundations.subtitle: Thirty decibels of copper loss means the receiver sees three per cent of the voltage, and the bits still arrive.
foundations.tldr: A serial link at today's rates throws away almost all of its signal in a few centimetres of copper and then rebuilds the bits anyway. The rebuilding is three machines in series: an analog filter shaped to cancel the channel's roll-off, a digital filter that mops up what is left, and an error-correcting code that fixes what neither filter caught. Every architectural argument in high-speed I/O — four voltage levels instead of two, digitise-then-equalise, co-packaged optics — is a trade among those three.

sections.heading: Thirty decibels of copper
sections.body_md:
Start with the number everything else follows from. A copper trace is a low-pass filter, and it loses signal two ways: conductor loss, because current crowds into the skin of the conductor as frequency rises, and dielectric loss in the insulating material around it, which grows faster still. Both get worse with distance, and neither can be designed away — they are properties of metal and plastic.

Now put a rate on it. A 112 Gb/s link using four voltage levels sends 56 billion symbols a second, so the frequency content that matters tops out near 27 GHz. A recently published 7 nm receiver works over a channel with **29.6 dB of insertion loss** at that frequency, and reaches a bit error rate of 6 × 10⁻⁹. Converting decibels to amplitude, 29.6 dB is a factor of about 30 in voltage: roughly three per cent of what the transmitter sent arrives at the receiver pin. The comparison table in the same paper reaches 48 dB, about a factor of 250, or four parts in a thousand. The eye at the pin is not small. It is closed.
sections.deeper_md: Insertion loss is quoted at the Nyquist frequency because that is where the worst-case pattern lives: alternating symbols at half the symbol rate. A receiver working into a channel quoted at over 40 dB there — which is what the 224 Gb/s generation is being designed against — is not sampling a signal in the ordinary sense. It is reconstructing one from a superposition of many neighbouring symbols, and the 30-tap feed-forward equaliser in the 7 nm design is a direct measure of how many. That is why insertion loss, rather than amplitude, is the unit a link budget is written in.

sections.heading: Why four levels, and what they cost
sections.body_md:
The obvious way to double a link's bit rate is to double the symbol rate, which doubles the Nyquist frequency and walks straight into the loss curve described above. PAM4 does something else: it sends two bits per symbol by using four amplitude levels instead of two, so a given bit rate needs only half the symbols per second and therefore half the bandwidth.

Nothing is free. Dividing the same peak-to-peak swing into four levels leaves three decision thresholds with one-third the spacing a two-level signal would have, which costs a factor of three in signal amplitude for the same noise — 20 log₁₀3, about **9.5 dB** of signal-to-noise ratio, as arithmetic rather than measurement. PAM4 wins anyway, because over the octave of bandwidth it saves, a real channel loses considerably more than 9.5 dB. That is the whole argument, and it is why the next step is being considered in the same terms: moving a 224 Gb/s interface to PAM4 needs roughly twice the analog front-end bandwidth, while PAM6 needs about 1.5 times.
sections.deeper_md: The trade is quantitative, so it can be checked rather than asserted. Across one octave of bandwidth a real channel of this class loses far more than 9.5 dB: the 7 nm receiver's own comparison set spans 29.6 dB to 48 dB of insertion loss at Nyquist, and the 224 Gb/s generation is being designed against channel libraries quoted at over 40 dB. Halving the Nyquist frequency buys back a large share of that, which is why PAM4 displaced two-level signalling rather than coexisting with it — and why the next move is argued in exactly the same currency, with PAM6 needing about 1.5 times the analog front-end bandwidth at 224 Gb/s against PAM4's 2 times.

sections.heading: Three equalisers, and what each cannot do
sections.body_md:
Equalisation means applying the inverse of the channel. It arrives in three flavours, and the useful way to hold them apart is by what each one cannot fix.

A **continuous-time linear equaliser** is an analog filter whose gain rises with frequency, cancelling the channel's roll-off before anything is sampled. The 7 nm receiver above tunes up to **17.5 dB of peaking at 27 GHz while holding its DC gain fixed** — it is reshaping the response, not amplifying everything. Its limit is that it is linear: noise and crosstalk at high frequency get boosted exactly as much as the signal.

A **feed-forward equaliser** is a sampled FIR filter — a weighted sum of neighbouring samples. That receiver uses **30 taps**; its cited predecessors use 16, 31 and 32. Being linear, it inherits the same noise problem.

A **decision-feedback equaliser** escapes it. Instead of filtering the measured waveform, it subtracts the known contribution of symbols already decided, so it cancels trailing interference without amplifying any noise. Two prices: it cannot touch interference from symbols not yet decided, and one wrong decision injects a wrong correction into the next.
sections.deeper_md: That last failure mode is called error propagation, and it is the reason DFE taps are kept few — one, in each of the four receivers compared in that paper — while FFE taps run to thirty. The deeper fix is sequence detection: rather than deciding symbol by symbol, score whole candidate sequences against the channel's known response. Maximum-likelihood sequence detection is the limit case, and it is being pulled into 224 Gb/s receivers precisely because 40+ dB channels defeat the filter-then-slice approach. It is also computationally brutal, and the Viterbi implementation has its own error-propagation behaviour in severe channels.

sections.heading: The error floor moved into the FEC
sections.body_md:
No link at these rates is error-free at the slicer, and the industry stopped pretending otherwise. Ethernet's answer at 400 Gb/s is a Reed–Solomon code written RS(544,514) and known as KP4: a codeword of 544 ten-bit symbols carrying 514 symbols of data, which leaves 30 parity symbols and the ability to repair **up to 15 errored symbols per codeword**. A link running a raw bit error rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ can be made effectively error-free behind it.

The condition attached to that sentence is where the engineering is. It holds only if the errors are random. A burst longer than 15 symbols exhausts the code, and then the whole codeword and every Ethernet frame inside it is lost. So the question stops being *how many* errors and becomes *how they clump* — and the named sources of clumping are the clock-recovery circuit, the multiplexers, long runs of identical symbols, and the decision-feedback equaliser's error propagation from the previous section. The equaliser's weakness reappears as the code's.
sections.deeper_md: This is why a raw bit error rate is a poor acceptance number: bursts are rare, so they barely move the average, and a link can measure 2 × 10⁻⁴ while failing. The measurement that distinguishes the two is the distribution of errors per codeword — how many 544-symbol blocks carry 0, 1, 2 … errored symbols — which shows directly how much of the 15-symbol correction budget is being consumed, and whether the margin is thin. Test equipment now defines burst at the bit, the PAM4 symbol and the FEC symbol level separately for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: The power bill for a wire
sections.body_md:
The reason this subject keeps producing architectural arguments is that none of the above is cheap. The 7 nm receiver reports **3.15 pJ per bit excluding its DSP**, in 0.195 mm² of die. At 112 Gb/s that is about 0.35 W for one lane's front end, by arithmetic — and the lane count on a switch die runs into the hundreds. The 10 nm design it compares against spends 4 pJ/bit in 0.281 mm², and the generational improvement in energy per bit is clearly slower than the increase in rate.

That ratio is the pressure behind every proposal to stop driving long copper. Co-packaged optics shortens the electrical run by putting the optical engine on the switch package; linear-drive optics goes after the module's own signal processing. Both are attempts to buy back picojoules that the equalisation chain spends. A research demonstration of eight lanes at 225 Gbaud driven by a 3 nm CMOS SerDes into thin-film lithium niobate modulators reached 3.2 Tb/s over 2 km — a preprint, and a laboratory result, but it is the direction the energy argument points.
sections.deeper_md: Energy-per-bit figures need reading carefully. The 3.15 pJ/bit above explicitly excludes DSP power, and in this receiver the DSP is where most of the equalisation happens: the analog front end supplies peaking, then a digital CTLE, a 30-tap FFE and a 1-tap DFE run on the digitised samples. A whole-link number that also carried the FEC decoder and the transmitter would be a different and larger figure, so a comparison across papers only means something when each states the boundary of what it measured — and three of the four designs in that comparison table report power while the fourth does not.

sections.heading: What the standards actually pin down
sections.body_md:
Two document families govern this, and conflating them causes real confusion. The Optical Internetworking Forum publishes the **Common Electrical I/O** implementation agreements, which specify the electrical and jitter behaviour of the interface between chips; the current one is OIF-CEI-05.3, dated July 2025, covering lane rates of 6G, 11G, 25G, 56G and 112G and above. IEEE 802.3 publishes the Ethernet side: the **P802.3dj** task force is defining 200 Gb/s, 400 Gb/s, 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s Ethernet, built from higher per-lane rates, as successor to the 802.3df work.

Hold on to the distinction. CEI tells you what a transmitter and receiver must do to interoperate across a specified channel; 802.3 tells you what an Ethernet port is. Neither is the same thing as shipping silicon: a published agreement states what interoperability requires, not that any particular part meets it.
sections.deeper_md: The useful property of the OIF index is that it is versioned and dated in public, so the rate list can be read as a timeline. CEI-03.0, September 2011, already listed 25G and above. 112G and above arrives with CEI-05.0 in May 2022 — eleven years later — and the list has not changed through 05.1 in December 2022, 05.2 in January 2024 and 05.3 in July 2025, which are revisions to the electrical and jitter requirements rather than new rates. Reading the version history is the cheapest available check on how fast the electrical interface actually moves, as distinct from how fast a roadmap slide says it does.

glossary.definition: How much signal amplitude a channel removes, on a logarithmic scale: 20 dB is a factor of 10 in voltage, 30 dB about 30×, 48 dB about 250×. It is the unit a high-speed link budget is written in.

Half the symbol rate — the highest frequency content a signalling scheme produces, and conventionally the frequency at which channel loss is quoted, because the alternating-symbol pattern that lives there is the worst case.
Baud counts symbols per second, bit rate counts bits. They are equal for two-level signalling and differ by a factor of two for PAM4, which is the entire point of PAM4.
Four-level pulse-amplitude modulation: two bits per symbol encoded as four voltage levels, halving the bandwidth needed for a given bit rate at the cost of roughly 9.5 dB of signal-to-noise ratio.

Energy from one symbol smearing into the time slots of its neighbours, because the channel's impulse response is longer than one symbol period. Pre-cursor ISI leaks forward in time, post-cursor ISI trails behind.

An analog filter at the receiver input whose gain rises with frequency to cancel the channel's roll-off before sampling. Being linear, it amplifies high-frequency noise and crosstalk along with the signal.

An equaliser that subtracts the computed contribution of symbols it has already decided. It removes post-cursor ISI without boosting noise, but it cannot see pre-cursor ISI, and a wrong decision corrupts the following ones.
The Reed–Solomon code Ethernet uses at 400 Gb/s: 544 ten-bit symbols per codeword, 514 of data, correcting up to 15 errored symbols — and losing the entire codeword if a burst exceeds that.
Energy per transmitted bit, the standard efficiency figure for a link. Multiply by the bit rate to get watts: 3.15 pJ/bit at 112 Gb/s is about 0.35 W.

foundations.try_this: Open Sam Palermo's ECEN 720 course index at Texas A&M and read Lecture 8, "RX FIR, CTLE, DFE, & Adaptive Eq." Then do the arithmetic the lecture assumes: the Journal of Semiconductors receiver equalises a 29.6 dB channel at 27 GHz, so for a 1 V differential swing at the transmitter, work out how many millivolts reach the receiver pin. Compare that with the 17.5 dB of analog peaking the front end supplies, and you have the gap the 30-tap FFE and 1-tap DFE are left to close — a single division that explains why the receiver is mostly a filter and only incidentally a comparator.
